defaults.permitted_development: A straightforward internal cellar conversion in Scotland can often proceed without planning permission where the works do not materially affect the external appearance and do not create a separate dwelling. External lightwells, excavation and visible alterations change that position.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate basement height allowance. What matters is whether railings, lightwell upstands, retaining walls, guards or linked above-ground works become prominent externally.
rules.depth_rules: There is no standalone permitted development depth right for basement excavation. Digging down to create new underground volume or materially enlarge the basement usually needs its own planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: Basement works near a boundary need careful review where they introduce lightwells, retaining walls, drainage changes or substantial excavation close to adjoining structures.
rules.roof_rules: If the project also includes a rear extension, roof terrace, plant or roof alteration, those elements need their own assessment. A purely internal conversion does not usually create a separate roof issue.
rules.materials_rules: Visible elements such as front lightwell walls, railings, grilles, doors and paving should be designed as part of the existing house rather than as a bolt-on intervention. Heritage settings usually need the most restrained detailing.

rules.permitted_development: The easiest Scottish basement case is an internal conversion within the existing space. A new basement, new lightwell, separate accommodation or other material external change is much more likely to need planning permission.

rules.height_rules: Height only becomes an issue where the basement scheme creates visible above-ground elements. Railings, retaining walls, lightwell upstands and other external additions are usually the parts that need checking.
rules.depth_rules: Basement works in Scotland do not benefit from an automatic excavation right. Once the proposal creates new below-ground volume or pushes beyond the existing envelope, expect a distinct planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: The planning question is usually hardest at the boundary, especially if the proposal adds lightwells, railings, retaining walls or major excavation next to adjoining property. Structural and neighbour impacts often sit alongside the formal route.
rules.roof_rules: The roof is rarely the deciding issue for a purely internal basement conversion. It becomes relevant only where the overall scheme includes visible above-ground work affecting the roofline or roof surface.
rules.materials_rules: Where the basement proposal introduces visible external work, keep the materials quiet and well integrated with the dwelling. Front lightwell details, railings and entrance alterations usually need the most careful design.

restrictions.conservation_area: In Edinburgh, conservation area controls and site-specific planning conditions often make visible external work more sensitive than the national baseline. Check planning permission, listed building consent and building warrant requirements together.

rules.permitted_development: In Scotland, internal works that do not materially affect the building’s external appearance are not normally treated as development, so an internal basement conversion is often the simplest case. New excavation, a lightwell or a separate unit is different.

rules.height_rules: Basement projects are not governed by a simple height cap in Scotland. The practical question is whether any above-ground parts such as lightwell walls, guard rails or altered entrances materially change the outside appearance.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is often the core basement question, but Scotland does not give a simple dig-down allowance. Creating new underground volume or materially enlarging the basement footprint generally needs separate planning review.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary conditions matter most where the scheme cuts new lightwells, alters retaining structures or excavates close to neighbouring buildings. Planning, drainage and structural issues often need to be worked through together.
rules.roof_rules: A basement conversion does not usually raise its own roof question unless the wider project adds terraces, rooflights, plant or linked above-ground alterations. Those elements must be assessed separately.
rules.materials_rules: Most material concerns arise only where the scheme changes what you can see from outside. Lightwell linings, guard rails, paving and new joinery should be detailed as part of the host property rather than an obvious add-on.

rules.roof_rules: The roof is rarely the deciding issue for a purely internal basement conversion. It becomes relevant only where the overall scheme includes visible above-ground work affecting the roofline or roof surface.
